related.name: Audio Dynamic Range & Data Rate Calculator

method: RIAA equalization is the disc recording characteristic adopted in the 1950s and still used for vinyl: the cutter reduces low frequencies and boosts high frequencies, and the phono stage applies the inverse on playback. The curve is fixed by three time constants, 3180, 318 and 75 microseconds, which put its corners at 50.05 Hz, 500.5 Hz and 2122 Hz. The playback magnitude is sqrt(1 + (2 pi f T2)^2) divided by sqrt(1 + (2 pi f T1)^2) times sqrt(1 + (2 pi f T3)^2), with T1 = 3180 us, T2 = 318 us and T3 = 75 us, normalised so that 1 kHz is 0 dB. That gives the familiar shape: a flat bass shelf at about +19.3 dB below 50 Hz, a 6 dB per octave bass slope between 50 Hz and 500 Hz, a flat mid band from 500 Hz to 2122 Hz, and a 6 dB per octave treble roll-off above 2122 Hz that reaches about -19.6 dB at 20 kHz. The record curve is the exact inverse, so the same numbers are shown with the opposite sign as the cut applied to the master. The standard defines no upper limit above the 75 microsecond corner, so the treble slope continues; the 3.18 microsecond correction sometimes called the Neumann pole is not part of the standard and is not added here, and the withdrawn 1976 IEC amendment that added a 7950 microsecond pole near 20 Hz is not applied either. Amplitude ratio is the linear form of the same gain, 10^(dB / 20). The stage gain follows from the cartridge output at 1 kHz and the target line level as 20 log10(target / cartridge), and the output at any other frequency is that target multiplied by the ratio there, which is why a stage sized for 1 V at 1 kHz must swing about 9.2 V at 20 Hz. Inputs are limited to 1 to 100000 Hz, 0.05 to 20 mV of cartridge output and 50 to 20000 mV of target output; results outside 20 Hz to 20 kHz are labelled as an extrapolation. Everything is computed in the browser with no uploads, network access or storage.

sources.title: RIAA equalization: the playback characteristic is the inverse of the record pre-emphasis and is defined by the 3180, 318 and 75 microsecond time constants, that is 50.05 Hz, 500.5 Hz and 2122 Hz.
IEC 60098, Analogue audio disk records and reproducing equipment: the standardized playback equalization characteristic and its 20 Hz to 20 kHz range.
Lipshitz, S. P., On RIAA Equalization Networks, Journal of the Audio Engineering Society, 1979: the transfer function of the playback curve and the network synthesis that realises it.
Ballou, G. (ed.), Handbook for Sound Engineers: RIAA playback and record curves, and phono-stage gain budgeting from cartridge output to line level.
